title: Rate Limiting: Stop Bots Without Killing Users 🛡️
ig_caption:
Bots don’t “break” APIs… they overwhelm them.
How rate limiting keeps your users safe 🔥

- One bot + one real user hit the same API endpoint.
- With NO limits: the bot floods requests → 100% of users get served while the API is effectively down ✗.
- With rate limiting: the bucket detects abusive volume.
- The bot gets throttled (“Bucket: bot throttled”), while the real user keeps working (0% backend load spike, users fine) ✓.
- Outcome: you protect backend capacity, preserve latency SLOs, and degrade only the offender.

Production takeaway: Use per-client/per-key rate limits (IP + auth token) and prioritize good-user traffic when contention happens.

What’s your biggest rate-limit failure mode in production—wrong scope, bad thresholds, or lack of backoff/logging? Drop your war story.

fb_caption:
Rate limiting looks simple—until you connect it to real traffic patterns, backend constraints, and failure behavior. In the visual concept: one bot and one real user contend for the same API.

What happens with no limits:
- The bot monopolizes request capacity.
- Backend resources (threads/connection pools/CPU) get saturated.
- The system fails “globally,” so users get caught in the blast radius—effectively “API down” behavior.

What happens with rate limiting:
- A token-bucket (or similar) policy creates a per-identity quota.
- The abusive client rapidly exhausts its bucket and is throttled.
- Legitimate traffic remains within its allowed rate, so the API stays available for real users.

Architectural trade-offs to consider:
- Scope: rate limit per IP, per API key, per user, or per route. Too broad can block legitimate customers; too narrow can be bypassed.
- Fairness vs protection: throttling the offender preserves shared capacity, but you must decide whether to degrade by latency, HTTP 429s, or queueing.
- Accuracy and resilience: distributed systems need consistent accounting (or acceptable approximations) using Redis/edge providers; avoid centralized bottlenecks.
- Threshold tuning: bursty real users (mobile networks, retries) require thoughtful limits and backoff guidance to prevent self-inflicted outages.
- Observability: without metrics (429 rates, top offenders, saturation indicators), rate limiting becomes a black box.

Scalability & resilience best practice:
- Implement rate limiting at the edge (API gateway / ingress) and enforce per identity + per endpoint.
- Return explicit 429 responses with retry-after behavior, and log throttling decisions for tuning.
- Ensure your limits are aligned with backend SLOs (CPU/DB saturation thresholds) so throttling stops resource exhaustion early.

Question for practitioners: Are your current limits protecting backend saturation—or are they mostly acting as a band-aid after you already see latency and error spikes?
threads_caption:

No limit → API effectively dies. With buckets → bot throttled, users survive. 
Where do your rate limits live, and did you tune for retries/bursts? 🤔
